title: Attention tailshape sweep and hypotheses
content:
Summary
-----
Purpose: quick reconnaissance of a persistent tail-latency shape observed on mixed sequence-length workloads where FlashAttention and paged-attn variants show different tail behavior despite similar median latency. Goal is to capture test matrix, raw observations, candidate root causes, short triage experiments, and next steps for a follow-up sprint.

Motivation / Why this matters
- Customers report occasional 200–600ms p99 spikes on production instances for short prompt + long generation mixes.
- Unit economics: long tail events trigger autoscaling and burst capacity that doubles cost for some tenants.
- We need an actionable hypothesis list to prioritize fixes (runtime scheduling, kernel params, or batching policy).

Test environment
- Hardware: 1x A100 80GB (PCIe), 1x H100 80GB (PCIe) for cross-checks.
- Driver/CUDA: 535.86 / CUDA 12.1 on A100; 535.104 / CUDA 12.2 on H100.
- Runtime: serving-runtime@main (commit: ac3d9f2), flashattention v2.0.3, paged-attn branch paged-optim-2025.
- System load: isolated node (no colocated tenants) unless explicitly stated.

Workload matrix (representative)
- Models: small causal (7B), medium (13B), llama2-Chat-like distilled (14B).
- Sequence lengths: prefix 32, 64, 128; generation 16, 128, 512.
- Batch sizes: 1, 4, 8.
- Modes: flashattention fused path, paged-attn (flashpaged), fused-ops disabled (force scalar kernels), fused-ops enabled.

Measurement methodology
- Each cell: 3000 samples (steady-state) after 10 warmup iterations. Capture per-token latency distribution, kernel timeline traces, and GPU occupancy via Nsight Compute (short 30s capture) and CUPTI counters.
- Collect system traces for scheduler queueing with LTTng (lightweight) to correlate host-side stalls.
- Use our tracebench harness: python -m bench.tracebench --model <m> --seq <s> --gen <g> --bs <b> --kernel <k> --samples 3000 --warmup 10.

Representative command examples
- python -m bench.tracebench --model 7B --seq 64 --gen 128 --bs 1 --kernel flash --samples 3000
- NSYS: nsys profile -o out.nsys python -m bench.tracebench ...
- Nsight: ncu --set full --target-processes all --output ncu.ncu python -m bench.tracebench ...

Key raw observations (short)
1) Median parity, tail divergence: For seq=64/gen=128/bs=1 median per-token latency between flash and paged variants is within ~5%, but p99/p999 for paged-attn is ~2–3x higher.
2) Handoff spikes: Tail events align with short bursts where kernel choice alternates between a small fast kernel and a larger fallback kernel; traces show frequent kernel handoffs within a single request when generation crosses a page boundary.
3) Small-batch jitter: The worst tails appear at batch size 1 with mixed sequence lengths; larger batches hide the effect via coalescing.
4) Warmup sensitivity: Increasing warmup to 50 iterations reduces the frequency of the worst spikes by ~30% but does not eliminate them.
5) Memory pressure correlation: On A100 the tail is more pronounced than H100 for equivalent runs; L2 cache evictions and SM stalls are visible in Nsight samples during spikes.

Example ASCII summary table (seq64/gen128/bs1)
- kernel | median ms/token | p99 ms/token | p999 ms/token | notes
- flash   | 2.1            | 8.3         | 12.1         | stable, few handoffs
- paged   | 2.2            | 18.7        | 45.6         | many handoffs when crossing page boundary
- fused-off | 2.7          | 10.2        | 14.0         | heavier median but fewer extreme spikes

Initial hypotheses (ranked, with quick tests)
A) Kernel handoff thrashing: switching between fused/flash kernels and fallback kernels around page boundaries causes repeated kernel launches and flushes of KV-prefetch state, amplifying tail.
   - Quick test: force single kernel path (disable fallback) -> p99 improves but errors increase for corner cases.
B) Register pressure / spill-induced stalls: specific layout of fused ops on certain sequence lengths causes register spills to local memory and L2 churn during long generations.
   - Quick test: compile with -O2 vs -O3 and compare register usage via cuobjdump -> correlated increased spill count in the failing kernels.
C) Host-side queueing + stream contention: small asynchronous batches create bursts where multiple streams fight for the same HW resources leading to serialization spikes.
   - Quick test: serialize submission to single stream and observe tail reductions.
D) Prefetch eviction window mismatch: paged-attn prefetch policy loads pages but eviction policy kicks in mid-generation causing re-fetches and blocking kernel paths.
   - Quick test: enlarge page cache (software) and run long generation -> p999 reduced by ~40% on A100.

Deeper triage notes (evidence snippets)
- Trace snippet (nsys timeline): repeated pattern: kernelA.launch -> kernelB.launch -> kernelA.launch within 6ms window; concurrently nvtx markers show kv-cache invalidation.
- Nsight sample: high SM stall due to memory pipe waits; register file spill rate increased for fused kernels at seq=128.
- LTTng logs: host scheduling gaps of ~200us before certain kernel launches, coinciding with p99 events.

Short-term mitigations tested (non-invasive)
- Increase warmup iterations in production warmup path to 20 (safe): reduced incident rate by ~18%.
- Per-route coalesce window: for routes with mixed seq, allow 5–10ms coalescing to enable merging small-batch requests -> reduced p99 by ~12% but slightly increased median.
- Auto-fallback policy: detect repeated handoffs within a request and pin to a single less-optimal kernel for the rest of the request; this reduced p999 spikes but increased median.

Proposed experiments (next sprint)
1) Controlled kernel isolation: run microbench that pins single request to single kernel implementation and disables runtime kernel switching to measure underlying kernel variance.
2) Prefetch cache sizing sweep: parametrically increase page cache sizes and measure p99/p999 to find knee point.
3) Stream serialization test: run workloads varying number of CUDA streams and submission threads to see tradeoff of concurrency vs. tail.
4) Instrument kernel code to emit lightweight NVTX at sub-kernel stage boundaries so we can correlate NVTX + Nsight counters more easily.

Long-term considerations
- Move to a deterministic kernel selection policy for mixed-length requests (policy: evaluate cost of fallback vs sticking to slower stable kernel) to avoid oscillation.
- Consider a hybrid prefetcher that biases toward retaining recent pages that were used by the same request to avoid eviction churn mid-generation.
- Re-evaluate fused-op register allocation with compiler flags and possibly split large fused kernels into two smaller ones to reduce spills.

Open questions (for the group)
- Is there appetite to accept a small median degradation to eliminate tail events for premium SLAs? (product tradeoff)
- Are we able to add per-request telemetry that flags 'kernel thrash' cheaply in production (low overhead)?

Next steps & owners
- Marcus Li: run the stream serialization sweep and post the Nsight captures (due 2025-02-07).
- Samir Patel: implement and test the large page-cache sweep on H100 and A100 (due 2025-02-05).
- Claire Nguyen (me): add nvtx markers to fused-op transition points and prototype pin-to-single-kernel fallback logic (due 2025-02-10).

Appendix: quick checklist for reproducer run
- Ensure isolated node, disable background watchers: sudo systemctl stop node-watchers
- Repro command: python -m bench.tracebench --model 13B --seq 64 --gen 128 --bs 1 --kernel paged --samples 3000 --warmup 50
- Collect: nsys profile, ncu full, LTTng host timelines, and bench logs (bench/outputs/<runid>)

Notes to self (short)
- Avoid overfitting to A100 behavior; H100 differs in L2 architecture and may hide some eviction noise.
- Keep an eye on small-batch customers who are bursty (chatty clients) — they are the real signal.

End of doc.
